title: Whose AI Will Rule The World? | NOEMA
gist: A Noema essay argues China's AI ambitions are rooted in a 3,500-year-old civilizational 'source code' of pattern-based thinking (oracle-bone script) that meshes naturally with neural networks and state-directed planning, while the Trump administration's science adviser Michael Kratsios is explicitly importing Chinese-style centralized, mission-driven science funding (Genesis Mission, X-Labs, 'golden tickets') to compete, even as critics call this an erosion of open Western science and a copy of Chinese state capitalism now being applied to firms like Anthropic.

themes.theme: Chinese Linguistic Source Code And AI Affinity

insights.claim: The ideographic Chinese writing system, which emerged roughly 3,500 years ago at Yinxu as a 'huge mental map of interlocking patterns,' created a civilizational cognitive style built on optimized visual pattern-juxtaposition that the author argues finds its 'ultimate realization' in neural networks, giving China a structural cultural affinity for algorithmic/AI thinking.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: Suggests China's societal embrace of AI-driven planning may be more culturally frictionless than the West's — a soft cultural-moat argument for weighing the speed of China's AI institutional adoption versus the US.
insights.quote: A civilization whose thinking has always been about the optimized, visual juxtaposition of concepts finds its ultimate realization in the neural network.

insights.claim: Chinese five-year economic plans are framed by the author as direct descendants of Shang-dynasty oracle-bone divination: not probabilistic economic forecasts but 'magical, state-directed inscriptions designed to conjure a reality into existence,' implying Chinese industrial policy operates partly on a symbolic willed-reality logic rather than pure analytic forecasting.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: Reframes China's target-driven industrial policy (including its AI+ plan) as goal-conjuring rather than probability-weighted forecasting — helps explain Beijing's willingness to over-commit capital to state-picked technology winners regardless of near-term ROI uncertainty.
insights.quote: Like today’s five-year plans, the oracle bones were not economic forecasts; they were magical, state-directed inscriptions designed to conjure a reality into existence.

insights.claim: Archaeologist and calligrapher You Shou, persecuted during the Cultural Revolution as one of Harbin's 'eight weirdos,' showed through analysis of oracle-bone and bronze inscriptions that the Chinese Communist Party was not a radical break from China's ancient hierarchical, ritual-driven elite culture but an 'unwitting captive' of it — a claim politically dangerous enough that the Party sought to crush her work.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: Implies deep continuity between imperial-era state-directed control mechanisms and today's CCP tech governance — relevant context for why China's current AI/tech statecraft resembles ancient patterns of centralized, ritualized state planning rather than a modern invention.
insights.quote: The Communist project had to crush scholars like You Shou because her work revealed that the Party was not a radical break from the past, but an unwitting captive of it.

themes.theme: Quantum Computing As China's Scientific Sovereignty Model

insights.claim: Pan Jianwei, working in Nobel laureate (2022 physics) Anton Zeilinger's lab, was part of the team that achieved the world's first experimental demonstration of quantum teleportation in 1997, and by 2016 he had built Micius, China's quantum-communication satellite — establishing him as China's leading quantum computing figure and a likely future Nobel candidate.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific individual and institutional lineage (Zeilinger lab -> Micius -> Hefei) behind China's quantum program — a concrete name/entity to track for quantum-computing policy and Nobel-related signaling.
insights.locator: For the past few months, I’ve been corresponding

insights.claim: QuantumCTek, a commercial quantum-technology firm founded by Pan Jianwei's academic research team, received a 23% equity stake investment from state-owned China Telecom specifically to build 'unhackable' national communications infrastructure based on Pan's proprietary hardware.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: A concrete state-owned-enterprise-to-lab commercialization pipeline to track: QuantumCTek/China Telecom quantum-comms infrastructure buildout is a template for state-backed quantum encryption plays that could reshape secure-communications infrastructure ahead of Western equivalents.
insights.locator: His work and influence extend far beyond university walls

insights.claim: Pan Jianwei is not a Communist Party member (his political affiliation is the minor, legally sanctioned Jiusan Society) but under Xi Jinping's 'sci-tech self-reliance' mandate he receives large, discretionary funding transfers without going through competitive grant cycles, making him an example of a new class of 'politically untouchable' scientist-entrepreneurs treated like venture-capital-backed founders rather than grant applicants.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: Signals China's science-funding model rewards demonstrated bottleneck-breaking talent with capital-allocation authority resembling VC funding — a structural speed advantage versus Western peer-review-gated grant funding that investors comparing US/China deep-tech funding cycles should weigh.

insights.so_what: Confirms encryption-breaking quantum risk as an explicit named US national-security concern — watch quantum-resistant cryptography adoption timelines and US-China quantum policy as a near-term geopolitical flashpoint.

insights.claim: The author analogizes quantum computing versus classical computing to Chinese characters versus the Roman alphabet: both achieve the same underlying function but through radically different architectures, implying China's differently-structured approach to computation could reach parity or advantage without converging on Western technical methods.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: Frames China's quantum bet as a genuinely alternative technical paradigm rather than a catch-up effort — relevant for assessing whether Chinese quantum investment could produce non-obvious architectural advantages rather than simply replicating Western approaches later.
insights.quote: quantum computing is to computing what Chinese characters are to the Roman alphabet: Both apparently fulfill the same function, but the way in which they do so is radically different.

themes.theme: US Science Policy Pivots Toward The Chinese Model

insights.claim: Michael Kratsios — a Thiel Capital and Tsinghua University alumnus now serving as Trump's science adviser — has authored a report the author calls the biggest revision to American science policy since Vannevar Bush's 1945 'Science: The Endless Frontier,' representing a shift away from decentralized, peer-reviewed Western academic science toward a centralized, mission-driven, state-backed model that mirrors Beijing's tech-governance approach.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: Signals a structural change in how US federal science funding will be allocated; investors in R&D-dependent sectors (deep tech, biotech, quantum) should watch for new funding mechanisms bypassing traditional peer review.
insights.quote: the biggest revision to American science policy since Vannevar Bush’s postwar “Science: The Endless Frontier,”
insights.locator: Michael Kratsios is an alumnus of arguably the two

insights.claim: The Kratsios report critiques traditional consensus-driven peer review as slow and conservative and proposes 'golden tickets' that let individual, state-appointed reviewers unilaterally fund highly ambitious, high-risk proposals without requiring consensus approval — a mechanism the article says already effectively exists for elite Chinese scientists like Pan Jianwei.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: Watch which US agencies adopt 'golden ticket' discretionary funding — it could accelerate specific high-risk bets (quantum, AI, biotech) and create outsized winners among favored labs and founders outside normal grant competition.
insights.quote: golden tickets" that empower individual, state-appointed reviewers to unilaterally fund highly ambitious, high-risk proposals without consensus approval.

insights.claim: The centerpiece initiatives of the Kratsios report — the 'Genesis Mission' and a new NSF 'X-Labs' program — are explicitly structured as 'Manhattan Project-style' efforts to build multidisciplinary independent research organizations applying AI directly to scientific productivity, bypassing legacy academic boundaries, and are modeled directly on China's National Laboratories and State Key Laboratories (e.g., Pan Jianwei's Hefei quantum facility, Fudan University's Xuemin Institute).
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: Track Genesis Mission and X-Labs funding announcements as leading indicators of where US federal AI-for-science capital will flow, and which institutions get bypassed versus favored.

insights.claim: Applying Peter Thiel's 2014 'Zero to One' framework — which contrasted China's 'definite pessimism' (comprehensive planning against anticipated disaster) with 1950s America's 'definite optimism' (belief the future would be bright by default) — the author argues that, as AI changes everything, the Chinese now appear more optimistic than Americans, an inversion of Thiel's original mapping.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: A sentiment/conviction asymmetry between the two countries could translate into differential capital commitment and risk tolerance for AI-driven industrial bets — relevant to comparing US versus China AI-capex conviction and political durability of related spending.

themes.theme: China's AI+ Export Strategy And State-Directed Deployment

insights.claim: The China-ASEAN Artificial Intelligence Application Cooperation Center in Nanning, Guangxi showcases Chinese AI applications across agriculture, logistics, public safety, manufacturing, finance, healthcare and education specifically to invite leaders from Vietnam, Laos and Indonesia to adopt China's AI-driven development model, with the explicit pitch that China can replicate its domestic results for them.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: China is actively marketing turnkey state-AI governance and infrastructure packages to Global South governments — an export channel to track for Chinese AI/surveillance/agri-tech/fintech vendors' addressable market growth in Southeast Asia.
insights.quote: Look, we figured out how to use AI to make our farmers richer, our factories better, our streets safer. We can do that for you too.

insights.claim: Nanning's nominal GDP per capita sits at nearly $10,000 — double Vietnam's and nearly five times higher than Laos's or Cambodia's — a statistic China uses to demonstrate its regional development model's efficacy when courting neighboring Global South governments.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: A concrete comparative economic data point China uses as a persuasion tool in its Belt-and-Road-adjacent AI diplomacy toward ASEAN neighbors.

insights.claim: China's AI+ plan treats AI as a utility/commodity — comparable to electricity — deployed narrowly to solve concrete state-defined problems (lowering electricity costs, safeguarding food supply, delivering national healthcare) rather than as an open-ended general-purpose technology, reflecting an application-first rather than frontier-research-first state approach to AI.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: Chinese AI investment likely concentrates in applied vertical infrastructure (agriculture, healthcare, logistics) rather than frontier model races — implies different investable themes (industrial AI, robotics, applied vertical SaaS) compared to the US's frontier-lab-centric AI investment pattern.
insights.quote: AI is understood as a tool, or perhaps a commodity like electricity, and the Chinese plan is to use that tool to solve Chinese problems.

insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: Illustrates a soft compliance/legitimacy cost Chinese tech firms bear — public alignment with the state's civilizational narrative — relevant to assessing political risk and public messaging behavior of Chinese AI companies.

insights.so_what: Frames a governance/political-economy risk factor for US AI policy — watch whether AI regulatory and ownership structures shift power toward big-tech incumbents versus the broader public, which could invite backlash or new regulation.

insights.so_what: Signals that China's state science establishment officially frames deep-tech research investment (quantum, AI, materials) as patient long-horizon capital rather than short-cycle applied ROI — relevant when modeling the time horizon of Chinese state deep-tech funding commitments.

insights.claim: Pan Jianwei told the author that China's government operates on the belief chain that 'technological change creates economic change creates political change,' and sees the world on the brink of a broad technological revolution spanning AI, quantum computing, biotech, new energy sources and materials science — framing Chinese state strategy as a coordinated multi-domain deep-tech push rather than an AI-only bet.
insights.speaker: JACOB DREYER
insights.so_what: Chinese state capital allocation is diversified across several simultaneous deep-tech domains, not concentrated solely on AI — useful for modeling the breadth (versus narrowness) of Chinese state-backed technology bets relative to the US's more AI-concentrated capex cycle.
